one_liner: SSE 4.1 16-stream interleaved 24-bit range decoder for order-0 bytes; on book1 it decodes about 1.6x faster than FSE tANS.
what_it_does: An order-0 static-model range coder (Pavlov/Subbotin style, 24-bit state, 12-bit probabilities) for 8-bit alphabets, split across 16 interleaved streams so that the decoder can run 4 SSE vectors of 4 lanes. The API is buffer-to-buffer: call vrange_init() once, build scaled cumulative frequencies with vrange_create_cum_probs(), encode with vrange_encode(vector, vector, cum_probs), build a 4096-entry lookup table with vrange_init_table() and decode with vrange_decode(src, comp_size, dst, orig_size, table). There is no container format in the library; frequency-table storage is up to the caller (the test app stores 256 16-bit frequencies, 512 bytes).
how_it_is_fast: The decoder's per-symbol division (value / (range >> 12)) is done four lanes at a time with _mm_div_ps on floats, which is exact because state values are kept under 24 bits; the quotient indexes a 4096-entry table packing symbol, low and frequency. Renormalization is branchless: two compare masks per vector form an 8-bit index into precomputed pshufb tables that shift each lane's state and splice in 0, 1 or 2 bytes from one 8-byte load. The encoder runs 16 scalar range coders and then swizzles their bytes into decode order, using the per-symbol byte counts it recorded, so the decoder needs no stream offsets.
when_to_use: Decode-heavy order-0 byte entropy coding on x86-64 with SSE 4.1, where decode speed matters far more than encode speed (encode is 51.9 MiB/s on the vectorized path).
You want a range coder rather than ANS because of patent concerns about ANS, the reason the author gives for the project.
Inputs of tens of kilobytes or more, so the 48-byte stream header (16 lanes x 3 bytes) and the scalar tail are amortized.
As a reference design for vectorized range decoding with float division and pshufb renormalization, small enough (about 700 lines) to vendor under the Unlicense.
when_not_to_use: Non-x86 targets: the decoder is written with SSE 4.1 intrinsics (_mm_insert_epi32, _mm_mullo_epi32, _mm_shuffle_epi8) and has no scalar or NEON fallback for the vectorized path.

Encode-bound workloads: the encoder is scalar, buffers 16 std::vector streams plus a per-symbol byte-count array (about one extra byte per input byte) and then swizzles, and the author says it is not optimized.
You need adaptive or higher-order models: probabilities are a single static 12-bit table per buffer.

Maximum single-core decode speed: FSE's Huff0 mode decodes book1 faster (800.9 MB/s on the same machine) and SIMD rANS siblings run several times faster; the AVX-2 64-stream port quoted at 1,373 MiB/s is not in the repo.
Untrusted input without your own bounds slack: the author writes that corruption safety is 'still testing', and the end-of-input guard is miscomputed (see gotchas).

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library (std::vector) and x86 intrinsic headers; packagemerge.c is used only by the test app for Huffman size comparisons
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMakeLists sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11, -O3 -msse4.1); author tested clang 10 and gcc 9.3.0 on Linux and clang, MSVC 2019 and MSVC 2022 on Windows
integration.thread_safety: not documented; vrange_init() fills global shuffle tables and must run before any use, after which encode and decode keep their state on the stack or in caller buffers

gotchas: The lookup tables (g_shift_shuf, g_dist_shuf, g_num_bytes, g_byte_shuffle_mask) are declared static in sserangecoder.h, so each translation unit gets its own copy and vrange_init() only fills the copy in sserangecoder.cpp; calling the inline low-level vrange_decode/vrange_normalize helpers from your own .cpp, as the README suggests, would use zeroed tables.

In vrange_decode(), pSrc_end is computed as pSrc + comp_size after the 48 initial state bytes have been consumed, so the end-of-input checks are 48 bytes too lax and comp_size >= 48 is not checked; on corrupt input the decoder can read past the buffer (the test app's wrapper only checks comp_size >= 48).

The encoder appends 2 zero padding bytes and the vectorized loop does 8-byte loads, so streams produced elsewhere need the same padding; the output buffer is written through a uint32_t* cast (4 symbols at a time).
Frequencies are rescaled to a 4096 total, with every used symbol getting at least 1, so very skewed distributions lose some precision versus 15-16-bit-probability coders.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ryg_rans or rans-tricks when you want a range coder (no ANS) with SSE 4.1 decode at about 580-620 MiB/s on book1; pick hypersonic-rANS, rans_static or htscodecs when ANS is acceptable and you have AVX2/AVX-512, since they decode several times faster, and FiniteStateEntropy's Huff0 when a slightly larger output is fine.
verified_claims_summary: On book1 (768,771 bytes) on a Core i7 1065G7 Ice Lake laptop, the 16-stream SSE 4.1 decoder ran at 552-619 MiB/s (8 rounds of 100 warm-cache decodes, 2.3-2.6 cycles/byte), against 370.3 MB/s decode for Collet's FSE demo and 512.8-565.6 MB/s for ryg_rans exam_simd_sse41 run separately under Linux clang; the range coder's compiler is not named, output was 436,229 bytes versus FSE 437,232 and ryg SIMD rANS 435,626, and FSE's Huffman mode decoded faster at 800.9 MB/s.
status_note: Abandoned since 2023-05-12 (85 commits, all three issues closed) but Unlicense and small enough to vendor; it is wired into powturbo's TurboBench as a plugin.
